subject: math
cluster: Represent and solve equations and inequalities graphically
description: Students graph the solution set of a linear inequality in two variables as a half-plane: they graph the boundary line (solid for $\le$ or $\ge$, dashed for $<$ or $>$), decide which side to shade by testing a point, and recognize that every point in the shaded region satisfies the inequality. They extend this to a system of linear inequalities, graphing each half-plane and identifying the solution set as the overlapping intersection region. They also verify whether a given ordered pair is a solution by substitution.
subSkills: Decide whether the boundary line is solid ($\le$, $\ge$) or dashed ($<$, $>$) from the inequality symbol
Graph the boundary line from slope-intercept or standard form
Choose a test point not on the line (usually the origin) and substitute to decide which half-plane to shade
Shade the correct half-plane for a single inequality
Verify whether an ordered pair is a solution of an inequality by substitution
Graph a system of two or more linear inequalities and identify the intersection of the half-planes as the solution region
Determine whether a point is a solution of a system (must satisfy every inequality)
Set up and graph a system of inequalities from a real-world constraint problem and interpret the feasible region

problemArchetypes.name: Solid vs. dashed boundary
problemArchetypes.example: For $y \ge 2x - 3$, state whether the boundary line $y = 2x - 3$ is solid or dashed and why. (Solid, because $\ge$ includes the boundary.)

problemArchetypes.name: Test-point shading (slope-intercept form)
problemArchetypes.example: Graph $y < \frac{1}{2}x + 1$. Draw the boundary dashed, test the point $(0,\,0)$: $0 < 1$ is true, so shade the side containing the origin.

problemArchetypes.name: Test-point shading (standard form)
problemArchetypes.example: Graph $2x + 3y \le 6$. Test $(0,\,0)$: $0 \le 6$ is true, so shade the origin side; the boundary $2x + 3y = 6$ is solid.

problemArchetypes.name: Verify an ordered pair in one inequality
problemArchetypes.example: Is $(4,\,1)$ a solution of $y > -x + 2$? Substitute: $1 > -4 + 2 = -2$ is true, so yes.

problemArchetypes.name: Boundary through the origin (origin cannot be the test point)
problemArchetypes.example: Graph $y \le 3x$. Because $(0,\,0)$ is on the line, test another point such as $(1,\,0)$: $0 \le 3$ is true, so shade the side containing $(1,\,0)$.

problemArchetypes.name: System of two inequalities
problemArchetypes.example: Graph the system $\begin{cases} y \ge x - 1 \\ y < -2x + 4 \end{cases}$ and shade the overlapping region that satisfies both.

problemArchetypes.name: Verify an ordered pair in a system
problemArchetypes.example: Is $(1,\,1)$ a solution of $\begin{cases} y \le 2x \\ y > -1 \end{cases}$? Check both: $1 \le 2$ true and $1 > -1$ true, so yes.

problemArchetypes.name: Real-world system of constraints
problemArchetypes.example: A student has at most $\$20$ to spend on apples at $\$2$ each and bananas at $\$1$ each, and wants at least $6$ pieces of fruit. Let $a$ and $b$ be the counts. Write and graph $\begin{cases} 2a + b \le 20 \\ a + b \ge 6 \\ a \ge 0 \\ b \ge 0 \end{cases}$ and describe the feasible region.

Easy.description: A single inequality already in slope-intercept form $y \,\square\, mx + b$ with small integer slope and intercept, where the origin $(0,\,0)$ is a valid test point. The student need only choose solid vs. dashed, test the origin, and shade. Also includes verifying an ordered pair in a single inequality by substitution.
constraints: Inequality given as $y < / \le / > / \ge \; mx + b$ with integer $m$ and $b$, $|m|, |b| \le 5$
Origin $(0,\,0)$ is not on the boundary, so it can be used as the test point
Boundary direction (solid/dashed) read directly from the symbol
Verification items substitute a single ordered pair into one inequality

Medium.description: The student must do setup before shading: rewrite an inequality from standard form $ax + by \,\square\, c$ into slope-intercept form (correctly FLIPPING the symbol when dividing by a negative), or handle a boundary through the origin where a non-origin test point is required. Also includes graphing a basic system of two inequalities in slope-intercept form and reading the overlap, plus checking a point against a system.
constraints: Inequality given in standard form and must be solved for $y$, possibly flipping the symbol when dividing by a negative coefficient
Boundary may pass through the origin, forcing a non-origin test point
Fractional slopes such as $\frac{2}{3}$ may appear
Systems of two inequalities both in slope-intercept form; identify the intersection region
Verify a point against a two-inequality system

Hard.description: Multi-step problems: systems of three or more inequalities (often including $x \ge 0$, $y \ge 0$ bounds), mixed standard and slope-intercept forms requiring rewriting and symbol-flipping, identifying a corner/vertex of the feasible region, or modeling a real-world constraint scenario by defining variables, writing every inequality, graphing the system, and interpreting the feasible region in context.
constraints: System of three or more inequalities, possibly with non-negativity constraints $x \ge 0$, $y \ge 0$
Mixed forms: some inequalities in standard form must be rewritten before graphing
May require finding a vertex of the feasible region by intersecting two boundary lines
Word problems require defining variables, writing each constraint as an inequality, and interpreting the feasible region
Must reason about strict vs. non-strict boundaries when deciding whether a vertex point is included

difficultyRubric.tierSplit: If split into two worksheets: tier1 covers Easy to Medium (solid vs. dashed, origin test-point shading from slope-intercept form, verifying ordered pairs, rewriting from standard form with symbol-flipping, and basic two-inequality systems). tier2 covers Medium to Hard (boundaries through the origin, three-or-more-inequality systems with non-negativity bounds, mixed forms, vertices of the feasible region, and full constraint word problems with interpretation). No item overlap between tiers.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Uses a solid line for a strict inequality or a dashed line for a non-strict one, mismatching the boundary style to the symbol
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Draws a solid boundary for $y > 2x - 3$ (should be dashed) or a dashed boundary for $y \ge 2x - 3$ (should be solid)

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Shades the wrong half-plane because the test point was substituted incorrectly or the true/false result was misread
commonMisconceptions.distractor: For $y < \frac{1}{2}x + 1$ tests $(0,\,0)$, gets the true statement $0 < 1$, but shades the side NOT containing the origin

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Forgets to flip the inequality symbol when dividing both sides by a negative coefficient while solving for $y$
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Rewrites $-2x + y < 4$... actually $2x - y \ge 4$ as $y \ge 2x - 4$ instead of $y \le 2x - 4$, shading the opposite half-plane

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Uses the origin as the test point when the boundary line passes through the origin, so the test gives an on-the-line result and no decision
commonMisconceptions.distractor: For $y \le 3x$ tests $(0,\,0)$, gets $0 \le 0$ (a point on the line), and shades arbitrarily instead of testing a point off the line

commonMisconceptions.misconception: For a system, shades the union of the half-planes (everything either inequality allows) instead of the intersection (only what both allow)
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Reports the combined shaded area of both inequalities as the solution instead of just the overlapping region

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Confuses slope and intercept when graphing the boundary, plotting $b$ as the slope or vice versa
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Graphs $y \ge \frac{2}{3}x + 1$ with slope $1$ and intercept $\frac{2}{3}$ instead of slope $\frac{2}{3}$ and intercept $1$

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Declares an ordered pair a solution of a system after checking only one inequality rather than all of them
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Calls $(1,\,1)$ a solution of $\begin{cases} y \le 2x \\ y > 3 \end{cases}$ because $1 \le 2$ holds, ignoring that $1 > 3$ is false
